sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Wireless networking uses radio signals instead of physical network cables to move information between devices.
For this objective, understand how wireless technologies differ by frequency, channel, channel width, frequency band, wireless standard, range, and purpose.
bullets: Wi-Fi frequencies: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz
Channels: regulations, selection, widths, frequencies, and bands
Bluetooth, near-field communication (NFC), and radio-frequency identification (RFID)
sections.callout: Frequency band → channels → channel width → performance and interference.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes range, interference, frequency, channel use, device pairing, proximity, or identification, can you recognize the wireless technology involved?
bullets: Longer range and better wall penetration → 2.4 GHz
More capacity and less congestion than 2.4 GHz → 5 GHz

sections.title: Wi-Fi Frequency Bands
paragraphs: Wi-Fi operates within defined portions of the radio-frequency spectrum. For this objective, know the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands.
In general, increasing frequency trades some propagation and obstacle penetration for additional spectrum and performance opportunities.
sections.callout: Lower travels better; higher gives Wi-Fi more room to work.

sections.title: 2.4 GHz
paragraphs: The 2.4 GHz band offers good range, better obstacle penetration than higher Wi-Fi frequencies, and broad device compatibility.
It is also crowded because many Wi-Fi and non-Wi-Fi devices share the spectrum, and it has fewer practical non-overlapping channel choices than 5 GHz.
sections.callout: 2.4 = reach farther, but crowded.

sections.title: 5 GHz
paragraphs: The 5 GHz band provides more available channels, less congestion than heavily used 2.4 GHz environments, support for wider channels, and strong performance opportunities.
Compared with 2.4 GHz, it generally has shorter practical range and less ability to penetrate obstacles.
sections.callout: 5 GHz = more room, less reach.

sections.title: 6 GHz
paragraphs: The 6 GHz band adds substantial spectrum for newer compatible Wi-Fi technologies. It offers more channels, room for wide channels, and less interference from older devices that cannot use the band.
Devices must specifically support 6 GHz, and its higher frequency makes range and obstacle penetration more challenging than lower-frequency Wi-Fi.
sections.callout: 6 GHz = new Wi-Fi territory for compatible equipment.

sections.title: 2.4 GHz vs. 5 GHz vs. 6 GHz

table.caption: Wi-Fi band recognition
rows: Better range and penetration; more congestion
More channels and capacity; shorter reach than 2.4 GHz
Additional newer spectrum; compatible equipment required

paragraphs: Higher frequency does not automatically guarantee a faster connection. Performance also depends on the Wi-Fi standard, signal quality, channel width, interference, client and access-point capabilities, distance, and obstacles.
sections.callout: 2.4 = reach; 5 = room; 6 = new room.

sections.title: Wireless Channels
paragraphs: A frequency band is divided into smaller portions called channels. Wi-Fi devices select channels within a supported band to communicate.
Nearby networks using the same or overlapping radio spectrum can interfere or compete with one another.
sections.callout: Band = where Wi-Fi lives; channel = where inside that band it talks.

sections.title: 2.4 GHz Channels
paragraphs: The 2.4 GHz band has limited channel space. In many common deployments, channels 1, 6, and 11 are the familiar non-overlapping 20 MHz choices.
Poor channel planning among nearby access points can create unnecessary competition and interference.
sections.callout: Common 2.4 GHz planning → 1, 6, 11.

sections.title: 5 GHz and 6 GHz Channels
paragraphs: 5 GHz provides considerably more channel choices than 2.4 GHz, and 6 GHz provides even more spectrum for compatible Wi-Fi technologies.
Available channels depend on regulatory region, equipment, channel width, and Wi-Fi implementation.
sections.callout: More spectrum provides more channel-planning options.

sections.title: Regulations
paragraphs: Governments regulate radio spectrum so devices and services can coexist. Channel availability and permitted operation can therefore vary by region.
A channel available in one country may be restricted elsewhere; equipment must be configured for the applicable regulatory requirements.
sections.callout: Channel unavailable because of geographic restrictions → regulations.

sections.title: Channel Selection
paragraphs: Channel selection affects interference, congestion, performance, and reliability. Nearby access points on the same channel must compete for the same radio space.
Selecting a cleaner appropriate channel can improve the wireless environment.
sections.callout: Do not make every access point shout in the same lane.

sections.title: Frequencies, Bands, and Channels

table.caption: Wireless terminology
rows: Rate of the radio signal, measured in hertz
A defined portion within a frequency band

sections.callout: Frequency = radio territory; band = neighborhood; channel = address inside it.

sections.title: Channel Width
paragraphs: Channel width describes how much radio spectrum a channel occupies. Common Wi-Fi widths include 20 MHz, 40 MHz, 80 MHz, and 160 MHz, depending on the technology and band.
A wider channel can provide more capacity, but it also consumes more spectrum. In crowded environments, narrower channels can preserve more independent channel opportunities.
sections.callout: Wide = more road, but it uses more land.

sections.title: Channel Width vs. Channel Number

table.caption: Channel number and width
rows: Where does communication occur inside the band?
How much spectrum does the channel occupy?

sections.callout: Number = where; width = how wide.

sections.title: 802.11 Standards
paragraphs: Wi-Fi networking is based on the IEEE 802.11 family of wireless LAN standards. Different generations support different combinations of frequency bands, speeds, channel widths, and wireless capabilities.
sections.callout: IEEE 802.11 = the Wi-Fi standards family.

sections.title: 802.11 Standard Recognition
sections.callout: b/g → 2.4; a/ac → 5; n → both; ax → modern multi-band Wi-Fi.

sections.title: Bluetooth
paragraphs: Bluetooth is short-range wireless technology used to connect nearby devices and peripherals such as headphones, speakers, keyboards, mice, and phones.
Bluetooth commonly operates in 2.4 GHz spectrum and can share radio space with other technologies there.
sections.callout: Nearby paired device or peripheral → Bluetooth.

sections.title: Bluetooth vs. Wi-Fi
sections.callout: Wi-Fi joins networks; Bluetooth joins devices.

sections.title: Near-Field Communication (NFC)
paragraphs: Near-field communication (NFC) provides wireless communication over an extremely short distance. Uses include contactless payments, access systems, reading compatible tags, and quick proximity interactions.
sections.callout: Tap or extremely close wireless interaction → NFC.

sections.title: Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID)
paragraphs: Radio-frequency identification (RFID) identifies or tracks tagged objects. An RFID tag holds identifying information, and an RFID reader detects that information.
RFID supports inventory tracking, asset identification, access cards, product tracking, and other identification systems.
sections.callout: Reader detects an identification tag → RFID.

sections.title: Active vs. Passive RFID

entries.title: Passive RFID
paragraphs: A passive tag has no active power source for normal transmission and uses energy from the reader's radio signal to respond.
entries.recognitionCue: Tag powered by reader interaction → passive RFID.

entries.title: Active RFID
paragraphs: An active tag has its own power source and can support greater capabilities and potentially longer ranges.
entries.recognitionCue: Tag has its own battery or power source → active RFID.

sections.callout: Passive borrows power; active brings power.

sections.title: NFC vs. RFID

table.caption: NFC and RFID recognition
rows: Extremely close interaction, payment, access, or tap
Identification and tracking with tags and readers

sections.callout: NFC = interact nearby; RFID = identify the tag.

sections.title: Wi-Fi vs. Bluetooth vs. NFC vs. RFID
sections.callout: Wi-Fi = network; Bluetooth = pair; NFC = tap; RFID = tag.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Better Wi-Fi range and penetration → 2.4 GHz
More Wi-Fi channel options than 2.4 GHz → 5 GHz
Nearby wireless LANs competing → channel selection

sections.title: Objective 2.2 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Wireless options can all be technically wireless. The job, distance, frequency, channel requirement, and environment determine the answer.

entries.title: 2.4 GHz vs. 5 GHz vs. 6 GHz
paragraphs: Do not automatically choose the highest number. Better range points to 2.4 GHz; more channel options point to 5 GHz; newer additional spectrum points to 6 GHz with compatible equipment.

entries.title: Band vs. Channel vs. Width
paragraphs: A band is a frequency range, a channel is a selected portion inside the band, and width is the amount of spectrum occupied.

entries.title: Wider Does Not Always Mean Better
paragraphs: Wide channels can increase potential throughput but consume more spectrum and can reduce reuse in a crowded environment.

entries.title: Bluetooth vs. Wi-Fi
paragraphs: Network connectivity points to Wi-Fi; peripheral pairing points to Bluetooth. Shared 2.4 GHz operation does not make them the same.

entries.title: NFC vs. Bluetooth
paragraphs: An extremely close tap points to NFC; a nearby paired accessory points to Bluetooth.

entries.title: NFC vs. RFID
paragraphs: A very-close interactive scenario points to NFC; an identification or tracking system points to RFID.

sections.callout: Ask: what is it doing, how far, what band, and what channel requirement?
